summary: Continuation of CA.1 (Residues and reciprocity), planned at target level from public sources. It supplies the four inputs the first pass left open. (1) The degree-n norm-residue symbol (a, b)_v = Art_v(a)(ⁿ√b)/ⁿ√b of a local field containing μ_n, moved down from K2SymbolsBrauer T.7 and built on Class Field Theory's local and archimedean Artin maps, with its global packaging at the places of a number field, bimultiplicativity, the Steinberg relation, skew symmetry, the norm criterion and nondegeneracy, functoriality, and the comparison with Class Field Theory's cohomological localSymbol (Fesenko–Vostokov IV.5, Milne III.4 and VIII.5); this is the symbol that CA.1's tame formula, degree-n product formula and power reciprocity law use. (2) Biquadratic reciprocity in ℤ[i]: primary Gaussian integers, the quartic Jacobi and Gauss sums of a primary prime, reciprocity with rational denominators and for coprime coordinates, the law (λ/π)_4 = (π/λ)_4 (−1)^{((Nλ−1)/4)((Nπ−1)/4)} for coprime primary elements, and the supplements for i, −1 and 1 + i, on the power residue symbol with n = 4 (Xu's REU paper, with the proofs it leaves to Ireland–Rosen written out; every formula checked by machine on small cases). (3) The three inputs of Eisenstein reciprocity: Φ(P) = g(P)^m, Stickelberger's relation (Φ(P)) = P^{Σ t σ_t⁻¹} (Katre, Clausen; the prime 2 supplied), the unit factor ±ζ_m^i and ±1 for primary α, the residue identity (Φ(P)/P')_m = (N P'/P)_m and Eisenstein reciprocity at ideal norms (Adhikari, Xu). (4) The number-field quadratic law with dyadic and archimedean factors, the completed symbol |α/β| and its periodicity modulo 8α (FIMR §2, Koymans–Milovic items 3–4), the norm compatibility of the power residue symbol in any finite extension, and the count 1 + (d/p) of zeros of a binary quadratic form on ℙ¹(𝔽_p) (Calegari–Geraghty adapter). Of the twelve first-pass targets whose obligations the independent review recorded, eight receive fourteen supporting lemma nodes (root counts, the squarefree part, primary Eisenstein integers, the cubic Jacobi and Gauss sums, the three cases of cubic reciprocity, its extension to rational denominators, and the normalising root of unity); the other four (the three degree-n theorems and Eisenstein reciprocity) are supplied by the norm-residue symbol and the Stickelberger nodes. A public proof of the 1 + i supplement and the value of the comparison sign ε remain, as recorded; the explicit laws at the places above n belong to HigherLocalFieldsAndHigherClassFieldTheory HL.4 (restructure entry).

nodes.title: The degree-n norm-residue symbol of a nonarchimedean local field
nodes.statement: Let F be a nonarchimedean local field, n ≥ 1, and suppose F contains a primitive n-th root of unity ζ (so the characteristic of F does not divide n and μ_n(Fˢ) ⊆ F). For a, b ∈ Fˣ choose β in a separable closure Fˢ with β^n = b; L = F(β) is a finite abelian (Kummer) extension of F. The degree-n norm-residue (Hilbert) symbol is (a, b)_{F,n} := Art_F(a)(β) / β ∈ μ_n(F), where Art_F(a) is the image of a under the local Artin map of Class Field Theory (Layer 6, localArtinMap for L/F; equivalently Layer 7, the absolute map artinMap F restricted to L), normalised by arithmetic Frobenius. The value does not depend on the root β, on the embedding of L in Fˢ, or on a and b beyond their classes in Fˣ/(Fˣ)^n.
hypotheses: n ≥ 1 and F contains a primitive n-th root of unity; this forces char F ∤ n, so X^n − b is separable for b ≠ 0.

Orientation is pinned: the first argument enters through the Artin map, the second through an n-th root. This is the orientation of Fesenko–Vostokov IV.5.1 and of Shastri §5; Milne's symbol (III.4, Remark 4.5; VIII.5.9) is the transpose, (a, b)_Milne = (b, a)_{F,n} = (a, b)_{F,n}⁻¹.
The Artin map is normalised by arithmetic Frobenius (Class Field Theory §2.6): a uniformiser acts on an unramified extension as x ↦ x^q on residues.
The value is an element of μ_n(F); no coordinate ζ is used in the definition, only in the comparison with the cohomological symbol.
proofSteps: Separability and Kummer theory: X^n − b is separable (Polynomial.separable_X_pow_sub_C, n a unit in F); since μ_n ⊆ F, L = F(β) is the splitting field of X^n − b (isSplittingField_X_pow_sub_C_of_root_adjoin_eq_top), so L/F is Galois, and σ ↦ σ(β)/β embeds Gal(L/F) in μ_n(F) (autAdjoinRootXPowSubCEquiv when X^n − b is irreducible; in general the same cocycle computation), so L/F is abelian.

The Artin symbol: Art_F(a) ∈ Gal(L/F)^ab = Gal(L/F) is localArtinMap F L ι a (Class Field Theory Layer 6); by artinMap_restrict (Layer 7) it is the restriction of the absolute symbol, and by localArtinEquiv_eq_of_iota it does not depend on the embedding ι. Set (a, b)_{F,n} := Art_F(a)(β)/β; it is an n-th root of unity of L, hence lies in μ_n(F).
Independence of β: another root is β' = ξβ with ξ ∈ μ_n(F), and Art_F(a) fixes ξ, so Art_F(a)(β')/β' = Art_F(a)(β)/β.

Dependence on classes: replacing b by b c^n replaces β by βc with c ∈ F, which Art_F(a) fixes; replacing a by a c^n multiplies Art_F(a) by Art_F(c)^n, which is trivial on L because Gal(L/F) has exponent dividing n.
acceptance: (7, 2)_{ℚ_7,3} is the cube root of unity of ℚ_7 congruent to 4 modulo 7, and (2, 7)_{ℚ_7,3} the one congruent to 2: the symbol is not symmetric, and the orientation is visible.
For n = 2 and F = ℚ_2, (−1, −1)_{F,2} = −1, the value of the quadratic norm-equation symbol.
For every a and every c, (a, c^n)_{F,n} = 1.

the power reciprocity law expresses (a/b)(b/a)⁻¹ as a product of these symbols at the places in S
for n = 2 the local factors μ₂ and μ_∞ are products of these symbols at the dyadic and archimedean places

nodes.title: The norm-residue symbol of ℝ and ℂ
nodes.statement: Let F be ℝ or ℂ (the completion of a number field at an infinite place) and n ≥ 1 with μ_n ⊆ F (so n ≤ 2 when F = ℝ). For a, b ∈ Fˣ and β ∈ ℂ with β^n = b, (a, b)_{F,n} := Art_F(a)(β)/β ∈ μ_n(F), where Art_F is the archimedean Artin map of Class Field Theory Layer 10 (infiniteArtinAt): trivial for F = ℂ, and for F = ℝ the map sending a to complex conjugation when a < 0 and to the identity when a > 0. Explicitly (a, b)_{ℂ,n} = 1, and (a, b)_{ℝ,2} = −1 exactly when a < 0 and b < 0; (a, b)_{ℝ,1} = 1.
hypotheses: F = ℝ or F = ℂ with its usual topology; μ_n ⊆ F.
Same orientation as the nonarchimedean symbol: the first argument through the Artin map.
proofSteps: Art_ℂ is trivial (infiniteArtinAt_eq_one_of_isComplex), so (a, b)_ℂ = 1.
Art_ℝ(a) is complex conjugation exactly when a < 0 (infiniteArtinAt_eq_one_iff_of_isReal); conjugation sends √b to −√b exactly when b < 0, so (a, b)_ℝ = −1 exactly when a < 0 and b < 0.
Bimultiplicativity, skew symmetry and the norm criterion follow from these values; for n = 2 the symbol agrees with the real quadratic norm-equation symbol of Global Quadratic Forms 4.4.
acceptance: (a, b)_{ℂ,n} = 1 for all n.

nodes.title: The degree-n norm-residue symbol at a place of a number field
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field containing a primitive n-th root of unity ζ. For a place v of K and a, b ∈ Kˣ, (a, b)_v := (a, b)_{K_v,n}, the norm-residue symbol of the completion K_v at the images of a and b: the nonarchimedean symbol at a finite place v (K_v = v.adicCompletion K, which contains ζ) and the archimedean symbol at an infinite place (K_v ≅ ℝ or ℂ; for n ≥ 3 every infinite place is complex because ζ is not real). The value lies in μ_n(K_v) = μ_n(K), identified through ζ.
hypotheses: K is a number field and ζ ∈ K is a primitive n-th root of unity, n ≥ 1.
Places are Mathlib's: finite places are IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K), infinite places are NumberField.InfinitePlace K.
proofSteps: At a finite place, K_v is a nonarchimedean local field containing the image of ζ; apply the local symbol.
At an infinite place, K_v is ℝ or ℂ; apply the archimedean symbol. If n ≥ 3, ζ ∉ ℝ, so no infinite place is real and every archimedean factor is 1.
μ_n(K) maps isomorphically onto μ_n(K_v) for every v, so all values can be read in μ_n(K).
acceptance: For K = ℚ, n = 2 and an odd prime p, (p, u)_p = legendreSym p u for a p-adic unit u, the reading of CA.1/hilbert-symbol.
For K = ℚ(ζ_3), n = 3 and the two primes 𝔭, 𝔭̄ above 7, (7, 2)_𝔭 (7, 2)_𝔭̄ = 1: complex conjugation exchanges the two places and inverts the value.

nodes.title: The norm criterion and nondegeneracy of the norm-residue symbol
nodes.statement: Let F be a nonarchimedean local field containing a primitive n-th root of unity, and a, b ∈ Fˣ. Then (a, b)_{F,n} = 1 if and only if a is a norm from F(β) (β^n = b), if and only if b is a norm from F(α) (α^n = a). Moreover (a, b)_{F,n} = 1 for every b if and only if a ∈ (Fˣ)^n, and (a, b)_{F,n} = 1 for every a if and only if b ∈ (Fˣ)^n; so the symbol induces a perfect pairing Fˣ/(Fˣ)^n × Fˣ/(Fˣ)^n → μ_n(F). For a subgroup A ⊇ (Fˣ)^n of Fˣ with orthogonal B = A^⊥, A is the norm group of F(ⁿ√B).
hypotheses: F nonarchimedean local, μ_n ⊆ F.
The second form uses skew symmetry (CA.1/norm-residue-symbol-steinberg-and-skew-symmetry).
proofSteps: (a, b) = 1 exactly when Art_F(a) fixes β, i.e. acts trivially on L = F(β); by local reciprocity (Class Field Theory Layer 6: the kernel of localArtinMap F L is the norm group N_{L/F}(Lˣ)), exactly when a ∈ N_{L/F}(Lˣ).
By skew symmetry (b, a) = (a, b)⁻¹, so (a, b) = 1 exactly when b is a norm from F(α).
If (a, b) = 1 for all a then N_{L/F}(Lˣ) = Fˣ; the index of the norm group equals [L:F] for the abelian extension L/F (Layer 6), so L = F and b = β^n ∈ (Fˣ)^n. Symmetrically for a.
Both sides being the finite group Fˣ/(Fˣ)^n, the pairing is perfect; the orthogonality statement is Fesenko–Vostokov's Theorem (5.2), deduced from the perfectness by counting.
acceptance: For F = ℚ_p with p odd and n = 2, (p, u) = 1 exactly when u is a square modulo p, i.e. when p is a norm from ℚ_p(√u).
In ℚ_7 with n = 3, (7, 2)_3 ≠ 1, so 7 is not a norm from ℚ_7(∛2), and 2 is not a cube in ℚ_7.

nodes.title: Bimultiplicativity, the Steinberg relation and skew symmetry of the norm-residue symbol
nodes.statement: Let F be a nonarchimedean local field containing a primitive n-th root of unity. For a, a', b, b' ∈ Fˣ: (a a', b) = (a, b)(a', b) and (a, b b') = (a, b)(a, b'); (1 − a, a) = 1 whenever a ≠ 1; (−a, a) = 1; and (b, a) = (a, b)⁻¹. The same identities hold for the archimedean symbol.
hypotheses: F nonarchimedean local containing μ_n; a ≠ 0 throughout, and a ≠ 1 in the Steinberg relation.
The identities are stated for the pinned orientation; they are invariant under transposition, so they hold verbatim for Milne's symbol.
proofSteps: Left multiplicativity: Art_F is a homomorphism and fixes μ_n(F) ∋ (a', b), so Art(aa')(β)/β = Art(a)(Art(a')(β))/β = (a, b)(a', b).
Right multiplicativity: with β₁^n = b, β₂^n = b', the product β₁β₂ is an n-th root of bb', and Art(a)(β₁β₂)/(β₁β₂) = (a, b)(a, b').

Steinberg: factor X^n − a = ∏ f_i into irreducibles over F; every root α_i generates the same field L = F(ⁿ√a) because the roots differ by elements of μ_n ⊆ F, so 1 − a = ∏ f_i(1) = ∏ N_{L/F}(1 − α_i) is a norm from L; by the norm criterion (second form) (1 − a, a) = 1.
Skew symmetry: 1 = (ab, −ab) = (a, −a)(a, b)(b, a)(b, −b) = (a, b)(b, a).
acceptance: In ℚ_7 with n = 3, (7, 2)(2, 7) = 1 (values congruent to 4 and 2 modulo 7).
(a, −a) = 1 gives (a, a) = (a, −1), so (a, a) = 1 when n is odd.

nodes.title: Functoriality of the norm-residue symbol in n, in the field and under isomorphisms
nodes.statement: Let F be a nonarchimedean local field containing a primitive n-th root of unity. (i) If F contains a primitive (nm)-th root of unity, then (a, b)_{F,nm}^m = (a, b)_{F,n}. (ii) For a finite separable extension L/F, a ∈ Lˣ and b ∈ Fˣ: (a, b)_{L,n} = (N_{L/F}(a), b)_{F,n}. (iii) For a continuous isomorphism of fields e : F ≃ F' (more generally σ ∈ Gal(Fˢ/F) with L ⊇ μ_n), e((a, b)_{F,n}) = (e a, e b)_{F',n}.
hypotheses: μ_n ⊆ F in (i)–(iii); μ_{nm} ⊆ F in (i).
In (ii) the symbol on the left is the symbol of L (which contains μ_n ⊆ F).
proofSteps: (i): if γ^{nm} = b then γ^m is an n-th root of b, and (Art(a)(γ)/γ)^m = Art(a)(γ^m)/γ^m.
(ii): the norm functoriality of the absolute Artin map (Class Field Theory Layer 7, artinMap_norm): the Artin symbol of a ∈ Lˣ restricted to F(β) is the Artin symbol of N_{L/F} a.
(iii): naturality of the absolute Artin map under isomorphisms (artinMap_congr, Layer 7), applied to an n-th root of b.
acceptance: (i) with n = 1: (a, b)_{F,m}^m = 1.
(ii) for a ∈ Fˣ ⊆ Lˣ and [L:F] = f: (a, b)_{L,n} = (a^f, b)_{F,n} = (a, b)_{F,n}^f, since N_{L/F}(a) = a^f.

nodes.title: The norm-residue symbol and Class Field Theory's cohomological local symbol
nodes.statement: Let F be a nonarchimedean local field containing a primitive n-th root of unity ζ, and let tr : H²(F, μ_n) ≃ ℤ/n be the invariant coordinate of Class Field Theory Layer 5 (h2MuEquivZMod_mixed). There is a sign ε ∈ {1, −1}, depending only on the conventions of kummerClass, of the cup product and of tr (not on F, n, ζ, a, b), such that for all a, b ∈ Fˣ: log_ζ (a, b)_{F,n} = ε · localSymbol (kummerCupPairing ζ) tr (kummerClass n F a) (kummerClass n F b) in ℤ/n, where log_ζ = muNRepEquivZMod ζ. The sign is fixed by one computation: for F unramified over ℚ_p with residue field of q ≡ 1 (mod n) elements, a uniformiser π and a unit u, the left side is the exponent k with ζ^k ≡ u^{(q−1)/n} (tame formula). For n = 2 the sign is irrelevant and the statement reads: (a, b)_{F,2} = −1 if and only if localSymbol (kummerCupPairing (−1)) tr (kummerClass a) (kummerClass b) = 1, Tau Ceti's localArtinMap_quadratic_eq_hilbertSymbol.
hypotheses: F nonarchimedean local, ζ ∈ F a primitive n-th root of unity; tr is the invariant coordinate, not an arbitrary isomorphism (localSymbol is stated in Class Field Theory with tr as a parameter; any other coordinate rescales the right side by a unit of ℤ/n).
The comparison is with the named pairing kummerCupPairing ζ; the zero pairing would make the right side vanish.
proofSteps: Milne (III.4, Remark 4.5) shows that the cup-product symbol of Kummer classes, read through the invariant, is the Artin-map symbol with its arguments transposed; by skew symmetry the transposition is the inverse, so the two symbols agree up to a sign of the coordinate.

Both sides are bimultiplicative and vanish exactly on norms (CA.1/norm-residue-symbol-norm-criterion; Class Field Theory's localSymbol_eq_zero_iff_mem_normGroup), and the sign is determined by the unramified computation, where the left side is the tame value and the right side is computed from the cyclic-algebra description of the cup of two Kummer classes (Layer 5, step 2 of the duality proof).
For n = 2 both sides are ±1-valued and the equivalence is Class Field Theory Layer 6's localArtinMap_quadratic_eq_hilbertSymbol.
acceptance: For n = 2 and F = ℚ_2: (−1, −1) = −1 and the cohomological symbol of (kummerClass (−1), kummerClass (−1)) is 1 ∈ ℤ/2.
The sign ε is the same for all local fields: it is fixed once, in the unramified case.

nodes.title: Primary Gaussian integers
nodes.statement: Let K = ℚ(i), given as a number field with IsCyclotomicExtension {4} ℚ K, and let i ∈ 𝓞_K be a primitive 4th root of unity, so that 𝓞_K = ℤ[i] with ℤ-basis {1, i}. An element α ∈ 𝓞_K is primary if α ≡ 1 (mod (1 + i)^3), that is, (1 + i)^3 divides α − 1 (the ideal ((1 + i)^3) = (2 + 2i) has norm 8). For α = a + bi with a, b ∈ ℤ this says: a ≡ 1 and b ≡ 0 (mod 4), or a ≡ 3 and b ≡ 2 (mod 4). If N(α) is odd (α prime to 1 + i), exactly one of α, iα, −α, −iα is primary. Primary elements are closed under products and complex conjugation; a rational integer is primary exactly when it is ≡ 1 (mod 4); a primary nonunit is a product of primary primes, which are the elements −q (q a rational prime ≡ 3 mod 4) and the primary elements of prime norm p ≡ 1 (mod 4); and for primary α = a + bi, (N(α) − 1)/4 ≡ (a − 1)/2 (mod 2). The predicate is stated for every element; the unit 1 satisfies it, so the reciprocity statements carry their nonunit hypotheses separately.
hypotheses: K = ℚ(i) with IsCyclotomicExtension {4} ℚ K and i ∈ 𝓞_K a primitive 4th root of unity; the coordinates a, b are those of the basis {1, i} (integralPowerBasisOfPrimePow).

Primary is the congruence modulo (1 + i)^3; it implies N(α) odd. Xu's Definition 5.4 adds 'nonunit' to the definition; here it is a hypothesis of the theorems, as for the parent's IsPrimaryEisenstein.
proofSteps: Coordinates: (1 + i)^3 = −2 + 2i = i(2 + 2i), and 1 + (2 + 2i)(x + yi) = (1 + 2x − 2y) + 2(x + y)i; so α = a + bi is primary exactly when a − 1 and b are even and (a − 1)/2 ≡ b/2 (mod 2), which is the stated pair of congruences mod 4.

Unique primary associate: the units of ℤ[i] are ±1, ±i (Zsqrtd.isUnit_iff_norm_isUnit). The group (𝓞_K/(1 + i)^3)ˣ has order 4 and is represented by 1, i, −1, −i, which are pairwise incongruent; so for N(α) odd the class of α is the class of exactly one of them, u⁻¹, and uα is the unique primary associate.
Closure under products and conjugation: immediate from the congruence, since (1 + i)^3 𝓞_K is stable under conjugation (1 − i = −i(1 + i)).

Factorisation: each prime factor of a primary nonunit has a unique primary associate; the product of these associates is primary and differs from α by a unit u with u ≡ 1 mod (1 + i)^3, so u = 1. The primary primes: −q for q ≡ 3 mod 4 (GaussianInt.prime_iff_mod_four_eq_three_of_nat_prime) and the primary associates of the factors of p = ππ̄ ≡ 1 mod 4 (GaussianInt.sq_add_sq_of_nat_prime_of_not_irreducible).

Norm congruence: if a ≡ 1, b ≡ 0 (mod 4), then a² − 1 ≡ 0 (mod 8) and b² ≡ 0 (mod 16), so (N − 1)/4 ≡ (a² − 1)/4 ≡ (a − 1)/2 (mod 2); if a ≡ 3, b ≡ 2 (mod 4), then (a² − 1)/4 is even and b²/4 is odd, and (a − 1)/2 is odd.
acceptance: −3, −1 + 2i (norm 5) and 3 + 2i (norm 13) are primary; 3, 1 + 2i and 1 + i are not.
The two primary primes above 5 are −1 + 2i and −1 − 2i, conjugate to each other.

nodes.title: The quartic symbol of a rational integer at a coprime rational integer is trivial
nodes.statement: Let K = ℚ(i). For a rational integer a that is odd and not a unit, and a rational integer m coprime to a, the quartic residue symbol at the ideal a𝓞_K is trivial: (m / a)_4 = 1.
hypotheses: a, m ∈ ℤ, a odd with |a| > 1, gcd(a, m) = 1.
The symbol is the parent's power residue symbol with n = 4 at the ideal a𝓞_K, which is prime to 2.
proofSteps: Reduce by multiplicativity in the ideal to a = p a prime.
If p ≡ 1 (mod 4), p = ππ̄ with π a Gaussian prime; by Galois equivariance under complex conjugation, (m/π̄)_4 = conj((m/π)_4) = (m/π)_4⁻¹, so (m/p)_4 = 1.
If p ≡ 3 (mod 4), p is prime in ℤ[i] with norm p²; (m/p)_4 ≡ m^{(p²−1)/4} = (m^{p−1})^{(p+1)/4} ≡ 1 (mod p) by Fermat, and the reduction of μ_4 modulo p is injective, so (m/p)_4 = 1.
acceptance: (3 / (−1 + 2i))_4 = i and (3 / (−1 − 2i))_4 = −i, whose product (3/5)_4 is 1 (checked by direct computation in 𝔽_5): the factors are not trivial, only their product.

sources.match: States and proves that χ_a(α) = 1 for coprime rational a, α with a odd and not a unit, by the split and inert cases.

nodes.title: The supplementary laws for i and −1
nodes.statement: Let K = ℚ(i) and let λ = a + bi be primary with N(λ) odd. Then (i/λ)_4 = i^{−(a−1)/2} and (−1/λ)_4 = (−1)^{b/2} = (−1)^{(a−1)/2}, the symbols being taken at the ideal λ𝓞_K. In particular, for a rational integer n ≡ 1 (mod 4), (i/n)_4 = (−1)^{(n−1)/4} and (−1/n)_4 = 1.
hypotheses: λ primary (possibly composite, possibly a rational integer); for λ = 1 both sides are 1.
i is the primitive 4th root of unity fixed in the definition of primary; replacing i by −i changes both sides compatibly.
proofSteps: Prime case, split: for a primary prime π = a + bi of norm p ≡ 1 (mod 4), (i/π)_4 = i^{(p−1)/4} by the value of the power residue symbol at a root of unity (powerResidueSymbol_zeta); and (p − 1)/4 ≡ −(a − 1)/2 (mod 4) by the coordinate congruences of a primary element (a ≡ 1, b ≡ 0 or a ≡ 3, b ≡ 2 mod 4).
Prime case, inert: for π = −q with q ≡ 3 (mod 4), (i/q)_4 = i^{(q²−1)/4} and (q²−1)/4 ≡ (q + 1)/2 = −(a − 1)/2 (mod 4).

Multiplicativity: the left side is multiplicative in λ (powerResidueSymbolIdeal_mul_right); the right side α ↦ i^{−(a−1)/2} is multiplicative on primary elements, a congruence check on (a, b) modulo 8; primary nonunits are products of primary primes.
−1 = i², and (−1)^{(a−1)/2} = (−1)^{b/2} for primary a + bi.
acceptance: Checked by direct computation for every primary prime with |a|, |b| ≤ 12 and for 67 primary composites with |a|, |b| ≤ 30.

sources.match: Proves (i/n)_4 = (−1)^{(n−1)/4} for rational n ≡ 1 mod 4 from the split and inert prime cases and multiplicativity; the node extends the same computation to all primary λ.
The quartic residue character χ_π(α) ≡ α^{(Nπ−1)/4} at a Gaussian prime, which gives the prime case.

nodes.title: The Jacobi sum of the quartic character of a primary prime
nodes.statement: Let π be a primary prime of ℤ[i] of norm p ≡ 1 (mod 4), and χ = (·/π)_4 the quartic residue character of 𝓞_K/π ≅ 𝔽_p, with values in 𝓞_K. Then −χ(−1) J(χ, χ) = π; equivalently J(χ, χ) = −(−1)^{(p−1)/4} π.
hypotheses: π prime, primary, of norm p ≡ 1 (mod 4); χ has order exactly 4 (orderOf_powerResidueSymbol).
J is Mathlib's jacobiSum with χ(0) = 0.
proofSteps: Middle term and pairing: in J = Σ_t χ(t)χ(1 − t) the term t = 1/2 is χ(1/4) = χ(4)⁻¹ = χ(−1), because −4 = (1 + i)^4 is a 4th power; the remaining t ∉ {0, 1, 1/2} pair as t ↔ 1 − t, each pair contributing 2u with u a unit, and 2u ≡ 2 modulo (2 + 2i) = ((1 + i)^3).
Hence J ≡ χ(−1) + (p − 3) ≡ χ(−1) + 2 and −χ(−1)J ≡ −1 − 2 ≡ 1 modulo (1 + i)^3 (using 4 ∈ (1 + i)^3): −χ(−1)J is primary.
Norm: J(χ, χ) J(χ⁻¹, χ⁻¹) = p (jacobiSum_mul_jacobiSum_inv; χ, χ and χ² are nontrivial) and J(χ⁻¹, χ⁻¹) is the complex conjugate of J(χ, χ); so −χ(−1)J is a primary element of norm p, hence π or π̄.

Divisibility: modulo π, χ(t) ≡ t^k with k = (p − 1)/4, so J ≡ Σ_t t^k (1 − t)^k, a sum of power sums Σ_t t^j with 1 ≤ j ≤ 2k < p − 1, each zero (FiniteField.sum_pow_lt_card_sub_one); so π divides J, and since π and π̄ are not associate, −χ(−1)J = π.
acceptance: For π = −1 + 2i (p = 5): χ(−1) = −1 and J(χ, χ) = −1 + 2i = π (direct computation).
Checked by direct computation for every primary split prime with |a|, |b| ≤ 12.

sources.match: States −χ_π(−1) J(χ_π, χ_π) = π for primary π (deferring the proof to Ireland–Rosen §9.9); the proof steps here follow the cubic argument of Xu Proposition 4.8 (p. 12).

nodes.title: The fourth power of the quartic Gauss sum
nodes.statement: Let π be a primary prime of ℤ[i] of norm p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and χ = (·/π)_4, pushed along an injective ring homomorphism φ : 𝓞_K → R into an integral domain R, and ψ a primitive additive character of 𝓞_K/π ≅ 𝔽_p with values in R. Then g(χ, ψ)^4 = p · φ(J(χ, χ))^2 = φ(π)^3 φ(π̄).
hypotheses: As in the Jacobi sum lemma; ψ primitive; R a domain (for example ℂ, or the ring of integers of ℚ(i, ζ_p), which the reciprocity proof uses for congruences modulo q).
proofSteps: g(χ)^2 = J(χ, χ) g(χ^2) (jacobiSum_mul_nontrivial with χ·χ = χ² ≠ 1).
χ² is the quadratic character of 𝔽_p and χ²(−1) = χ(−1)² = 1, so g(χ²)^2 = p (gaussSum_sq).
Hence g(χ)^4 = p J(χ, χ)^2, and J(χ, χ)^2 = π² by the Jacobi sum lemma; p = ππ̄. Transport along φ is termwise (MulChar.ringHomComp).
acceptance: |g(χ, ψ)|² = p in ℂ (gaussSum_mul_gaussSum_eq_card), consistent with |π³π̄| = p².

sources.match: States g(χ_π)^4 = p J(χ_π, χ_π)^2 and the consequence g(χ_π)^4 = π³π̄.
The Gauss–Jacobi relation g(χ)g(λ) = J(χ, λ)g(χλ) and g(χ)g(χ̄) = χ(−1)p used in the steps.

nodes.title: Quartic reciprocity between a primary element and a rational integer
nodes.statement: Let K = ℚ(i). (a) For an odd rational prime q and a primary prime π of ℤ[i] of norm p ≡ 1 (mod 4) with p ≠ q: ((−1)^{(q−1)/2} q / π)_4 = (π / q)_4. (b) For a rational integer a ≡ 1 (mod 4) and a primary λ ∈ ℤ[i] coprime to a: (a / λ)_4 = (λ / a)_4.
hypotheses: Symbols are the parent's power residue symbols with n = 4 at the principal ideals (π), (q), (λ), (a), all of odd norm.
In (b), λ may be composite or rational; a may be negative.
proofSteps: (a), q ≡ 3 (mod 4): q is inert, 𝓞_K/q ≅ 𝔽_{q²} with Frobenius x ↦ x^q acting as complex conjugation, so π^q ≡ π̄ and (π/q)_4 ≡ π^{(q²−1)/4} = (π̄/π)^{(q+1)/4} (mod q). In R = 𝓞 of ℚ(i, ζ_p): g(χ_π)^q ≡ Σ χ(t)^q ψ(t)^q = Σ χ̄(t) ψ(qt) = χ(q) g(χ̄) (mod q) (gaussSum_frob, gaussSum_mulShift_eq), so g^{q+1} ≡ χ(q) g(χ)g(χ̄) = χ(q)χ(−1) p; and g^{q+1} = (π³π̄)^{(q+1)/4} = π^{q+1}(π̄/π)^{(q+1)/4} ≡ p (π/q)_4 (mod q). Cancel p and lift from congruence modulo q to equality of 4th roots of unity: (π/q)_4 = χ_π(−q).

(a), q ≡ 1 (mod 4): q = λλ̄; g^q ≡ χ(q)⁻¹ g (mod q), so g^{q−1} ≡ χ_π(q)⁻¹; also g^{q−1} = (π³π̄)^{(q−1)/4} ≡ (π³π̄ / λ)_4 (mod λ) and likewise modulo λ̄; combining with Galois equivariance (conjugation exchanges λ and λ̄ and inverts values) gives χ_π(q) = (π/λ)_4 (π/λ̄)_4 = (π/q)_4.

(b): write a = ∏ q_j* with q_j* = (−1)^{(q_j−1)/2} q_j (the product of these factors is ≡ 1 mod 4 and equals ±a, hence a); for each primary prime factor λ_k of λ that is split, (a/λ_k) = ∏_j (q_j*/λ_k) = ∏_j (λ_k/q_j) = (λ_k/a) by (a); for an inert factor −q both sides are 1 by the rational lemma; multiply over k.
acceptance: ((−3)/(−1 + 2i))_4 = ((−1 + 2i)/3)_4 = −i, the instance of parent source issue E203 (direct computation).

sources.match: States (a) for an odd prime q (deferring the proof to Ireland–Rosen §9.9, which writes g^{q+1}, resp. g^{q+3}, in two ways) and proves (b) from (a) by multiplicativity; the steps here carry out the computation sketched there, as in the cubic case.

nodes.title: Quartic reciprocity for primary elements with coprime coordinates
nodes.statement: Let π = a + bi and λ = c + di be coprime primary elements of ℤ[i] with gcd(a, b) = gcd(c, d) = 1. Then (λ/π)_4 = (π/λ)_4 · (−1)^{((a−1)/2)((c−1)/2)}.
hypotheses: π, λ primary, coprime, nonunits or units; gcd(a, b) = gcd(c, d) = 1, so a, b, c, d are prime to π, λ as appropriate.
proofSteps: From c i ≡ d (mod λ): c π ≡ ac + bd (mod λ), so (c/λ)(π/λ) = ((ac + bd)/λ); from b i ≡ −a (mod π): a λ ≡ ac + bd (mod π), so (a/π)(λ/π) = ((ac + bd)/π).

Taking the complex conjugate of the second relation (Galois equivariance: conj((x/π)_4) = (x̄/π̄)_4) and combining it with the first expresses (π/λ)(λ/π)⁻¹ as a product of symbols whose numerators are the rational integers c, a and ac + bd; by the rational-denominator lemma each becomes a symbol with a rational denominator, and the congruences c + di ≡ di (mod c), a + bi ≡ bi (mod a) and π̄λ ≡ (ad − bc)i (mod ac + bd), with the rational lemma, reduce these to symbols of i.

Collecting, (λ/π)(π/λ)⁻¹ = (i / (ac + bd)ac)_4 = (−1)^{((ac+bd)ac − 1)/4} by the supplement for i, and ((ac + bd)ac − 1)/4 ≡ ((a − 1)/2)((c − 1)/2) (mod 2) for primary a + bi, c + di (casework mod 8; checked by machine for all primary pairs with |a|, …, |d| ≤ 21).
When a, c or ac + bd is ±1 the corresponding factor is 1 and the same computation applies.
acceptance: For λ = −3 (d = 0, gcd(−3, 0) = 3 ≠ 1) the lemma does not apply directly; the general theorem handles it by the decomposition λ = m(c + di).

sources.match: States and proves this case from the two congruences, the rational lemmas and the supplement for i, with the final congruence left to casework.

nodes.title: The law of biquadratic (quartic) reciprocity
nodes.statement: Let K = ℚ(i) and let λ, π ∈ ℤ[i] be coprime primary elements (in particular of odd norm). Then (λ/π)_4 = (π/λ)_4 · (−1)^{((N(λ)−1)/4)((N(π)−1)/4)}, the symbols being the quartic power residue symbols at the principal ideals (π) and (λ).
hypotheses: λ, π primary and coprime; for a unit (λ = 1) both sides are 1.
The quotient (λ/π)(π/λ)⁻¹, not the product, is the sign: the product is not a sign in general (parent source issue E203).
proofSteps: Write π = m(a + bi), λ = n(c + di) with m, n rational, m ≡ n ≡ 1 (mod 4), gcd(a, b) = gcd(c, d) = 1; then a + bi and c + di are primary (IsPrimaryGaussian.div_intCast).
By the rational-denominator lemma, (λ/m) = (m/λ) and (π/n) = (n/π); by the rational lemma (m/n) = (n/m) = 1.
Expand (λ/π) = (λ/m)(λ/(a + bi)) = (m/λ)(n/(a + bi))((c + di)/(a + bi)) and apply the coprime-coordinates lemma: (λ/π) = (π/λ)(−1)^{((a−1)/2)((c−1)/2)}.
Finally ((a − 1)/2)((c − 1)/2) ≡ ((N(π) − 1)/4)((N(λ) − 1)/4) (mod 2), from the norm congruence (N − 1)/4 ≡ (a − 1)/2 for primary elements and m² ≡ n² ≡ 1 (mod 8).
acceptance: π = −1 + 2i (norm 5) and λ = −3 (norm 9): (λ/π)_4 = (π/λ)_4 = −i, and the sign is (−1)^{1·2} = 1 (parent source issue E203).
Checked by direct computation for 266 coprime pairs of primary composites with |a|, |b| ≤ 30.
The sign is −1 exactly when N(λ) ≡ N(π) ≡ 5 (mod 8).

sources.match: States biquadratic reciprocity for relatively prime primary elements and proves it from Propositions 5.10–5.13 by the decomposition π = m(a + bi).

nodes.title: The supplementary law for 1 + i
nodes.statement: Let λ = a + bi ∈ ℤ[i] be primary. Then ((1 + i)/λ)_4 = i^{(a − b − b² − 1)/4}, the symbol being taken at the ideal λ𝓞_K. In particular, for a rational integer n ≡ 1 (mod 4), ((1 + i)/n)_4 = i^{(n−1)/4}.
hypotheses: λ primary (composite allowed); a − b − b² − 1 is divisible by 4 for primary a + bi.
proofSteps: Split prime π = a + bi, b ≠ 0: b i ≡ −a (mod π) gives b(1 + i) ≡ b − a (mod π), so ((1 + i)/π) = ((b − a)/π)(b/π)⁻¹. Write b = 2^k b' with b' odd and use (2/π) = (−i/π)((1 + i)/π)²; this gives ((1 + i)/π)^{1+2k} as a product of symbols of rational integers and of −i.

The rational symbols: for odd rational m with ±m ≡ 1 (mod 4), (m/π) = (±1/π)·(π/±m) (rational-denominator lemma); (π/b') = (a/b') = 1 since a + bi ≡ a (mod b'), and (π/(b − a)) = ((b(1 + i))/(b − a)) = ((1 + i)/(b − a)) since a ≡ b (mod b − a) and the rational lemma; ((1 + i)/q)_4 = (2i)^{(q² − 1)/8} modulo an inert q and ((1 + i)/p)_4 = i^{(p−1)/4} for split p = ρρ̄ (conjugation and 1 − i = −i(1 + i)).
Since 1 + 2k is odd, it is invertible modulo 4, which determines ((1 + i)/π); a congruence computation on a, b modulo 16 yields i^{(a − b − b² − 1)/4}. The inert primes π = −q are computed directly.

Both sides are multiplicative on primary elements (for the right side, a congruence check of α ↦ (a − b − b² − 1)/4 mod 4 on primary residues modulo 32, done by machine), and primary nonunits are products of primary primes.
acceptance: Checked by direct computation for every primary prime with |a|, |b| ≤ 12 and for 67 primary composites with |a|, |b| ≤ 30.

nodes.title: The Gauss sum power Φ(P) = g(P)^m of a prime of ℤ[ζ_m]
nodes.statement: Let m ≥ 2, K = ℚ(ζ_m) with ζ_m a primitive m-th root of unity, and P a prime of 𝓞_K = ℤ[ζ_m] not dividing m, lying over the rational prime p, with N(P) = q = p^f. On F = 𝓞_K/P let χ_P(t) = (t/P)_m⁻¹ (the inverse of the m-th power residue character, χ_P(0) = 0) and ψ(t) = ζ_p^{Tr_{F/𝔽_p}(t)}, and let g(P) = g(χ_P, ψ) ∈ ℚ(ζ_m, ζ_p). Then Φ(P) := g(P)^m lies in 𝓞_K. Extend Φ multiplicatively to nonzero ideals A prime to m: Φ(A) = ∏ Φ(P_i) for A = P_1 ⋯ P_r, with Φ(𝓞_K) = 1, and write Φ(α) = Φ(α𝓞_K) for α prime to m.
hypotheses: m ≥ 2; P ∤ m, equivalently p ∤ m; ζ_p ∈ ℚ(ζ_m, ζ_p) = ℚ(ζ_{mp}) a primitive p-th root of unity (for p = 2, ζ_2 = −1).
The character is the inverse of the residue symbol: with (·/P)_m itself the ideal of Φ(P) would be P^{Σ t σ_t} instead of P^{Σ t σ_t⁻¹}.
proofSteps: g(P) is an algebraic integer of ℚ(ζ_{mp}), with g(P) times its complex conjugate equal to q (gaussSum_mul_gaussSum_eq_card) in every complex embedding.

For c ≡ 1 (mod m) prime to p, the automorphism ζ_{mp} ↦ ζ_{mp}^c fixes ℚ(ζ_m) and multiplies g(P) by χ_P(c)⁻¹, an m-th root of unity (gaussSum_mulShift_eq); hence it fixes g(P)^m, and these automorphisms are Gal(ℚ(ζ_{mp})/ℚ(ζ_m)), so Φ(P) ∈ 𝓞_K.
Multiplicativity in A by definition, through the factorisation of A in the Dedekind domain 𝓞_K.
acceptance: For m = 2, K = ℚ and P = (p) with p odd: χ_P is the Legendre character and Φ((p)) = g² = (−1/p) p = (−1)^{(p−1)/2} p.
For m = 3 and P = (π) with π = −1 − 3ω primary of norm 7: Φ(P) = 7π̄ = π π̄², whose ideal is P^{1·σ_1⁻¹ + 2·σ_2⁻¹}.

nodes.title: Stickelberger's relation: the prime factorisation of Φ(P)
nodes.statement: Let m ≥ 2, K = ℚ(ζ_m), and P a prime of ℤ[ζ_m] not dividing m. Then the principal ideal generated by Φ(P) = g(P)^m is P^γ, where γ = Σ_{1 ≤ t < m, gcd(t, m) = 1} t σ_t⁻¹ ∈ ℤ[Gal(K/ℚ)], σ_t(ζ_m) = ζ_m^t, and P^{Σ a_σ σ} := ∏ σ(P)^{a_σ}. Consequently (Φ(A)) = A^γ for every ideal A prime to m, and (Φ(α)) = (α^γ) for α prime to m.
hypotheses: m ≥ 2; P ∤ m. The rational prime p below P may be 2 (when m is odd).
proofSteps: Teichmüller character: put q = N(P) = p^f and choose a prime 𝔓 of ℚ(ζ_{q−1}) above P; reduction modulo 𝔓 gives ω : 𝔽_qˣ → μ_{q−1}, and χ_P = ω^{−(q−1)/m} (Katre, after Proposition 2).

Valuation of Gauss sums: for the prime 𝔓̃ of ℚ(ζ_{q−1}, ζ_p) above 𝔓, v_𝔓̃(g(ω^{−α})) = s(α), the sum of the base-p digits of α ∈ [0, q − 1): from s(0) = 0, s(α + β) ≤ s(α) + s(β) and s(α + β) ≡ s(α) + s(β) (mod p − 1) (Jacobi sums are integral in ℚ(ζ_{q−1}) and 𝔓 = 𝔓̃^{p−1}), s(pα) = s(α), s(α) + s(q − 1 − α) = f(p − 1), and s(1) = 1 (g(ω⁻¹) ≡ ±(ζ_p − 1) modulo 𝔓̃², the sign depending on the sign convention for Gauss sums), by Katre's counting argument.

Galois conjugates of 𝔓̃ give the full factorisation of (g(χ_P)) in ℚ(ζ_m, ζ_p), and the digit-sum identity s(h) = (p − 1) Σ_{i<f} {p^i h/(q − 1)} turns m times it into the exponent Σ_{(t,m)=1, t<m} t σ_t⁻¹ on P = 𝔓̃^{p−1} ∩ 𝓞_K; unique factorisation descends the equality of ideals to 𝓞_K.

The prime p = 2 (possible when m is odd): Katre and Clausen take p odd. For p = 2, ζ_2 = −1, ℚ(ζ_m, ζ_2) = ℚ(ζ_m) and 𝔓̃ = 𝔓; with Tr(a) lifted to {0, 1}, (−1)^{Tr(a)} = 1 − 2 Tr(a), so g(ω⁻¹) = ±2 Σ ω⁻¹(a) Tr(a) and the sum is ≡ q − 1 ≢ 0 modulo 𝔓; since 2 is unramified in ℚ(ζ_{q−1}), s(1) = 1, and the rest of the argument is unchanged with p − 1 = 1 (source issue E1102).

nodes.title: The unit Φ(α)/α^γ is a root of unity ±ζ_m^i
nodes.statement: Let m ≥ 2, K = ℚ(ζ_m) and α ∈ 𝓞_K prime to m. Then Φ(α) = ε(α) α^γ for a unit ε(α) of 𝓞_K, and ε(α) = ±ζ_m^i for some i.
hypotheses: α nonzero and prime to m; α^γ := ∏_t σ_t⁻¹(α)^t.
proofSteps: By Stickelberger's relation (Φ(α)) = (α^γ), so ε(α) = Φ(α)/α^γ is a unit.
In every complex embedding, |Φ(α)|² = |N(α)|^m (stickelbergerPhi_norm_sq), and |α^γ|² = α^{γ(1 + σ_{−1})} = α^{m Σ_t σ_t⁻¹} = |N(α)|^m, since (1 + σ_{−1})γ = m Σ_t σ_t⁻¹; so |ε(α)| = 1.
Galois equivariance (σ(Φ(α)) = Φ(σα)) shows the same for every conjugate of ε(α); by Kronecker's theorem ε(α) is a root of unity, and the roots of unity of ℚ(ζ_m) are the ±ζ_m^i (torsionOrder_eq).

nodes.title: For primary α in ℤ[ζ_l], Φ(α) = ±α^γ
nodes.statement: Let l be an odd prime, K = ℚ(ζ_l), and α ∈ ℤ[ζ_l] primary (prime to l and congruent to a rational integer modulo (1 − ζ_l)²). Then ε(α) = ±1, that is Φ(α) = ±α^γ. Moreover Φ(P) ≡ −1 (mod l) for every prime P ∤ l, so Φ(A) ≡ ±1 (mod l) for every ideal A prime to l.
hypotheses: l an odd prime; α primary in the sense of CA.1/primary-element-of-a-cyclotomic-ring.
proofSteps: Φ(P) ≡ −1 (mod l): modulo l in ℤ[ζ_l, ζ_p], g(P)^l ≡ Σ_t χ_P(t)^l ψ(t)^l = Σ_{t ≠ 0} ψ(lt) = −1, since χ_P^l is trivial on 𝔽_qˣ and l is invertible in 𝔽_q; as Φ(P) ∈ 𝓞_K and l ℤ[ζ_l, ζ_p] ∩ 𝓞_K = l𝓞_K, Φ(P) ≡ −1 (mod l𝓞_K). Hence Φ(α) ≡ ±1 (mod l).

With λ = 1 − ζ_l and α ≡ x (mod λ²), x ∈ ℤ, every σ(α) ≡ x (mod λ²) because λ²𝓞_K is Galois stable; so α^γ ≡ x^{1 + 2 + ⋯ + (l−1)} = (x^{(l−1)/2})^l ≡ ±1 (mod λ²), using x^{(l−1)/2} ≡ ±1 (mod l) and l ∈ λ².

So ε(α) ≡ ±1 (mod λ²); by the previous lemma ε(α) = ±ζ_l^i, so ζ_l^i ≡ ±1 (mod λ²); the sign is + because ζ_l^i ≡ 1 (mod λ) and 2 ∉ λ, and then ζ_l^i ≡ 1 − iλ (mod λ²) forces l | i (the uniqueness of the normalising power, CA.1/normalising-root-of-unity-of-a-cyclotomic-integer). Hence ε(α) = ±1.
acceptance: For l = 3, (1 − ω)² = −3ω, so an element ≡ 2 (mod 3) such as π = −1 − 3ω (norm 7) is primary in this sense, and ε(π) = 1 by the computation Φ(π) = 7π̄ = π^γ.
The primary hypothesis is needed: for α = ζ_l π, Φ(α) = Φ(π) but α^γ = ζ_l^{Σ t·t⁻¹}π^γ = ζ_l^{l−1}π^γ ≠ ±π^γ.

nodes.title: The residue symbol of Φ(P) at a second prime
nodes.statement: Let m ≥ 2, K = ℚ(ζ_m), and P, P' primes of ℤ[ζ_m] not dividing m with N(P) and N(P') coprime. Then (Φ(P)/P')_m = (N(P')/P)_m.
hypotheses: P, P' ∤ m; gcd(N(P), N(P')) = 1, so P' does not divide Φ(P) (|Φ(P)|² = N(P)^m).
proofSteps: Let q' = N(P') = p'^{f'}, so q' ≡ 1 (mod m). Modulo p' in ℤ[ζ_m, ζ_p], the q'-th power map is additive, so g(P)^{q'} ≡ Σ_t χ_P(t)^{q'} ψ(t)^{q'} = Σ_t χ_P(t) ψ(q't) = χ_P(q')⁻¹ g(P) = (q'/P)_m g(P).
g(P) is invertible modulo p' (g(P) times its complex conjugate is N(P), which is prime to p'), so g(P)^{q'−1} ≡ (q'/P)_m (mod p').
On the other hand g(P)^{q'−1} = Φ(P)^{(q'−1)/m} ≡ (Φ(P)/P')_m modulo every prime above P' (defining congruence of the residue symbol).
Two m-th roots of unity congruent modulo a prime above p' ∤ m are equal (CA.1/norm-of-a-prime-is-one-modulo-n).
acceptance: For m = 3, P = (π) with N(π) = 7 and P' = (2): (Φ(P)/2)_3 = (7π̄/2)_3 = (π̄/2)_3 and (N(2)/π)_3 = (4/π)_3 = (2/π)_3²; both equal ω: modulo 2, π̄ = 2 + 3ω ≡ ω and 7 ≡ 1, and the residue symbol at the inert prime 2 is x ↦ x^{(4−1)/3} = x; modulo π, ω ≡ 2 in 𝔽_7 and 4^{(7−1)/3} = 16 ≡ 2.

nodes.title: Eisenstein reciprocity at the norm of an ideal
nodes.statement: Let l be an odd prime, K = ℚ(ζ_l), α ∈ ℤ[ζ_l] a primary nonunit, and 𝔅 an ideal of ℤ[ζ_l] prime to l with N(𝔅) prime to α. Then (α/N(𝔅))_l = (N(𝔅)/α)_l, the symbols at the principal ideals N(𝔅)𝓞_K and α𝓞_K.
hypotheses: l odd prime; α primary and not a unit; 𝔅 prime to l; N(𝔅) and α coprime.
proofSteps: Reduce by multiplicativity to 𝔅 = P prime.
(Φ(α)/P) = ∏_i (Φ(P_i)/P) over the prime factors P_i of α, and by the residue identity each factor is (N(P)/P_i); so (Φ(α)/P) = (N(P)/α).
(α^γ/P) = ∏_t (σ_t⁻¹(α)/P)^t = ∏_t σ_t((σ_t⁻¹α/P)) = ∏_t (α/σ_t P) = (α/∏_t σ_t(P)) = (α/N(P)), by Galois equivariance (σ_t acts on μ_l by the t-th power) and ∏_σ σ(P) = N(P)𝓞_K.
Φ(α) = ±α^γ (previous lemma), and (−1/P)_l = 1 because −1 = (−1)^l is an l-th power; combining, (α/N(P)) = (N(P)/α).

nodes.title: The completed quadratic residue symbol |α/β| of a number field
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field. For α, β ∈ 𝓞_K with α ≠ 0 and β odd (β𝓞_K prime to 2), put μ_∞(α, β) = ∏_{v | ∞} (α, β)_v and μ₂(α, β) = ∏_{v | 2} (α, β)_v, products of the degree-2 norm-residue symbols at the infinite and the dyadic places, μ(α, β) = μ₂(α, β) μ_∞(α, β), and define the completed quadratic residue symbol |α/β| := μ_∞(α, β) · (α/β), where (α/β) is the quadratic residue symbol at the ideal β𝓞_K (the power residue symbol with n = 2). If α or β is totally positive, or K is totally complex, then |α/β| = (α/β).
hypotheses: K a number field; −1 is a primitive square root of unity in 𝓞_K, so the power residue symbol with n = 2 is defined at every odd ideal.
α ≠ 0 so that the local symbols (α, β)_v are defined; |α/β| = 0 when α and β are not coprime.
β odd: β𝓞_K is prime to 2. The plain symbol (α/β) depends only on the ideal β𝓞_K; μ_∞, and hence |α/β|, also depends on the signs of β at the real places.
proofSteps: (α/β) is the parent's power residue symbol of the ideal β𝓞_K with n = 2, valued in {0, ±1}.
μ_∞ and μ₂ are finite products of degree-2 norm-residue symbols at places (CA.1/norm-residue-symbol-at-a-place), each ±1.
If α or β is totally positive, every real factor (α, β)_v is 1 (the archimedean symbol is −1 only when both are negative), and a complex factor is always 1.
acceptance: For K = ℚ and positive b, |a/b| is the Jacobi symbol (a/b).

nodes.title: Quadratic reciprocity in a number field with dyadic and archimedean factors
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field and α, β ∈ 𝓞_K nonzero, odd and coprime. Then (α/β) = μ(α, β) (β/α) with μ = μ₂ μ_∞, the products of the degree-2 norm-residue symbols over the dyadic and the infinite places; equivalently |α/β| = μ(α, β)|β/α| = μ₂(α, β)(β/α).
hypotheses: α, β nonzero, odd (prime to 2), and coprime; the quadratic residue symbols are at the ideals β𝓞_K and α𝓞_K.
proofSteps: Apply the power reciprocity law with n = 2 (−1 ∈ K is a primitive square root of unity): (α/β)(β/α)⁻¹ = ∏_{v | 2∞} (α, β)_v, since (α), (β) and (2) are pairwise coprime.
The values are ±1, so the inverse is the value itself, and the right side is μ₂(α, β)μ_∞(α, β).
The degree-2 symbol is symmetric ((β, α)_v = (α, β)_v⁻¹ = (α, β)_v), so μ_∞(β, α) = μ_∞(α, β); hence |α/β| = μ_∞(α, β)μ(α, β)(β/α) = μ₂(α, β)(β/α) = μ(α, β)|β/α|.
acceptance: For K = ℚ and odd positive coprime a, b: μ_∞ = 1 and μ₂(a, b) = (a, b)_2 = (−1)^{((a−1)/2)((b−1)/2)}, which is jacobiSym.quadratic_reciprocity.

nodes.title: The dyadic factor μ₂(α, β) depends only on α and β modulo 8
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field and α, β, α', β' ∈ 𝓞_K odd with α ≡ α' and β ≡ β' (mod 8𝓞_K). Then μ₂(α, β) = μ₂(α', β').
hypotheses: α, β, α', β' odd; congruences modulo 8𝓞_K.
proofSteps: If η ∈ 𝓞_K and η ≡ 1 (mod 8), then η is a square in K_v for every dyadic place v: the binomial series √(1 + 8x) = 1 + Σ_{ℓ≥1} c_ℓ (4x)^ℓ/ℓ!, c_ℓ = ∏_{0≤k<ℓ}(1 − 2k), converges 2-adically because 4^ℓ/ℓ! has positive 2-adic valuation (alternatively Hensel's lemma).

Write α' = αη with η = α'/α ≡ 1 (mod 8) in 𝓞_{K_v} (α is a v-adic unit); then (α', β)_v = (α, β)_v(η, β)_v = (α, β)_v, since (η, β)_v = 1 for a square η (bimultiplicativity and (c², β) = 1). The same for β.
acceptance: For K = ℚ: (a, b)_2 for odd a, b depends only on a, b mod 4 (it is (−1)^{((a−1)/2)((b−1)/2)}), a fortiori mod 8.
17 ≡ 1 (mod 8) is a square in ℚ_2, so μ₂(17α, β) = μ₂(α, β).

nodes.title: Periodicity of the completed quadratic residue symbol modulo 8α
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field and α ∈ 𝓞_K nonzero. For odd β, δ ∈ 𝓞_K with β ≡ δ (mod 8α), |α/β| = |α/δ|. If moreover β and δ are totally positive, (α/β) = (α/δ).
hypotheses: α ≠ 0; β, δ odd; congruence modulo the ideal 8α𝓞_K.
No coprimality is assumed: if α and β are not coprime then neither are α and δ, and both sides are 0.
proofSteps: For odd α the statement follows from the reciprocity law, |α/β| = μ₂(α, β)(β/α), since (β/α) depends only on β mod α and μ₂ only on β mod 8 (FIMR Corollary 2.4).

For α with 1 + α odd, the auxiliary symbol [α/β] = μ₂(α, β)|α/β| = μ(α, β)(α/β) satisfies [α/β] = [α/δ] when β ≡ δ (mod 2α): choose γ with βγ ≡ 1 + α (mod 2α) and λ = (βγ − 1)/α, odd and prime to βγ; apply the reciprocity law to (α/β) = (−λ/β) and to (β/λ), (λ/γ), and collect the local factors, which reduce to (βγ, α)_v by the Steinberg relation (βγ, −αλ)_v = (βγ, 1 − βγ)_v = 1 (FIMR Lemma 2.5).
Apply this to 2 and to 2α (both have 1 + (·) odd): [2/β] = [2/δ] for β ≡ δ (mod 4) and [2α/β] = [2α/δ] for β ≡ δ (mod 4α); multiplying, and since 4 is a square, [α/β] = [α/δ] for β ≡ δ (mod 4α).
For β ≡ δ (mod 8α), μ₂(α, β) = μ₂(α, δ) by the previous lemma, so |α/β| = |α/δ|; for totally positive β, δ, |α/·| = (α/·).
acceptance: For K = ℚ, |−1/b| = (−1)^{(b−1)/2} for every odd b, positive or negative: it depends only on b mod 4.
Without the archimedean factor periodicity fails: for K = ℚ, −3 ≡ 5 (mod 8), but (−1/−3) = −1 ≠ 1 = (−1/5), while |−1/−3| = 1 = |−1/5|.

nodes.title: Norm compatibility of the power residue symbol in an extension
nodes.statement: Let L/K be a finite extension of number fields, n ≥ 1, and suppose 𝓞_K contains a primitive n-th root of unity. For x ∈ 𝓞_K and a nonzero ideal 𝔄 of 𝓞_L with N(𝔄) prime to n, (x/𝔄)_{L,n} = (x/N_{L/K}(𝔄))_{K,n}, where N_{L/K} is the relative norm of ideals (Mathlib's Ideal.relNorm) and both symbols are the parent's power residue symbols of ideals. In particular, for w ∈ 𝓞_L with N(w) prime to n, (x/w)_{L,n} = (x/N_{L/K}(w))_{K,n}.
hypotheses: L/K any finite extension (no Galois hypothesis); μ_n ⊆ K, hence μ_n ⊆ L, with the same roots of unity used on both sides.
N(𝔄) prime to n, so N_{L/K}(𝔄) is prime to n (Ideal.absNorm_relNorm).
proofSteps: Both sides are multiplicative in 𝔄 (powerResidueSymbolIdeal_mul_right; relNorm is a monoid homomorphism), so reduce to a prime 𝔓 of 𝓞_L over 𝔭 of 𝓞_K, with residue degree f; then N_{L/K}(𝔓) = 𝔭^f (Ideal.relNorm_eq_pow_of_isMaximal) and N(𝔓) = N(𝔭)^f.
If x ∈ 𝔭 both sides are 0. Otherwise, modulo 𝔓, (x/𝔓)_L ≡ x^{(N𝔭^f − 1)/n} = (x^{(N𝔭 − 1)/n})^{1 + N𝔭 + ⋯ + N𝔭^{f−1}} ≡ ((x/𝔭)_K)^{f} because N𝔭 ≡ 1 (mod n) makes the exponent ≡ f (mod n).
((x/𝔭)_K)^f = (x/𝔭^f)_K, and two n-th roots of unity congruent modulo 𝔓 are equal (CA.1/norm-of-a-prime-is-one-modulo-n in L).
acceptance: If L/ℚ is Galois of even degree and p splits completely in L, then for a ∈ ℤ prime to p, (a/p𝓞_L)_{L,2} = (a/p)^{[L:ℚ]} = 1, although the Legendre symbol (a/p) may be −1 (FIMR §2, p. 5).

nodes.title: The number of zeros of a binary quadratic form on ℙ¹(𝔽_p)
nodes.statement: Let p be an odd prime and Q(x, y) = m x² + r x y + n y² with m, r, n ∈ 𝔽_p not all zero. The number of points [x : y] ∈ ℙ¹(𝔽_p) with Q(x, y) = 0 is 1 + (d/p), where d = r² − 4mn is the discriminant and (·/p) is the Legendre symbol with (0/p) = 0: there are 0, 1 or 2 zeros according as d is a nonsquare, zero, or a nonzero square.
hypotheses: p odd; Q is not the zero form (for the zero form every one of the p + 1 points is a zero).
d = r² − 4mn is the discriminant of the form, which equals −4 det of the symmetric matrix (m, r/2; r/2, n); the determinant itself gives a different Legendre symbol when p ≡ 3 (mod 4).
proofSteps: Q(λx, λy) = λ²Q(x, y), so vanishing at [x : y] is well defined on ℙ¹(𝔽_p) = ℙ(𝔽_p²).

m ≠ 0: [1 : 0] is not a zero (Q(1, 0) = m); every other point is [x : 1], a zero exactly when m x² + r x + n = 0, i.e. when (2mx + r)² = d (quadratic_eq_zero_iff_discrim_eq_sq, 2 ≠ 0); x ↦ 2mx + r is a bijection of 𝔽_p, so the count is #{s : s² = d} = 1 + (d/p) (quadraticChar_card_sqrts, legendreSym.card_sqrts).
m = 0, r ≠ 0: [1 : 0] is a zero and [x : 1] is a zero exactly for x = −n/r; two zeros, and d = r² is a nonzero square.
m = 0, r = 0: then n ≠ 0, Q = n y² vanishes only at [1 : 0]; one zero, and d = 0.
acceptance: Over 𝔽_3, x² + y² has no zeros (d = −4 ≡ 2 is a nonsquare); over 𝔽_5 it has two, [2 : 1] and [3 : 1] (d ≡ 1).
xy has the two zeros [1 : 0], [0 : 1] (d = 1); y² has the single zero [1 : 0] (d = 0).
Over 𝔽_3, x² + xy + y² (d = −3 ≡ 0) has the single zero [1 : 1].

sources.match: The proof of Lemma 8.21 uses that a p-primitive binary quadratic form has 0, 1 or 2 zeros in ℙ¹(𝔽_p) according as the Legendre symbol of its discriminant is −1, 0 or 1; the node is that fact for every nonzero form over 𝔽_p, with the discriminant r² − 4mn.

nodes.title: The number of n-th roots of an n-th power in a finite field
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements, n ∈ ℕ and a ∈ Fˣ an n-th power. Then the equation x^n = a has exactly gcd(q − 1, n) solutions x ∈ Fˣ. If n ≥ 1, every solution in F is nonzero, so x^n = a also has exactly gcd(q − 1, n) solutions in F. For n = 0 (where a must be 1) all q elements of F are solutions, one more than the gcd(q − 1, 0) = q − 1 solutions in Fˣ.
hypotheses: F finite with q elements; a ≠ 0 and a is an n-th power.
Root counts are taken in Fˣ; the count in F agrees for n ≥ 1 and differs by one (the root 0) for n = 0.
proofSteps: Fˣ is cyclic of order q − 1 (isCyclic_of_injective_ringHom, Nat.card_units).
If x₀^n = a, the solutions in Fˣ are x₀ times the kernel of the n-th power map, which has gcd(q − 1, n) elements (IsCyclic.card_powMonoidHom_ker).
For n ≥ 1, 0^n = 0 ≠ a, so no solution is zero; for n = 0, x^0 = 1 for every x ∈ F, including 0.
acceptance: In 𝔽_7, x³ = 1 has three solutions (1, 2, 4) and x³ = 6 has three (3, 5, 6); x³ = 2 has none.
In 𝔽_5 with n = 0 and a = 1: five solutions in F and four in Fˣ.

sources.match: For positive n and α ∈ Fˣ, x^n = α is solvable exactly when α^{(q−1)/d} = 1 (d = gcd(n, q − 1)), and then has exactly d solutions; the node pins the count in Fˣ and records the n = 0 boundary that the review flagged.

nodes.title: Uniqueness of the signed squarefree part of a rational square class
nodes.statement: If d, d' ∈ ℤ are squarefree, c, c' ∈ ℚ are nonzero, and d c² = d' c'² ≠ 0, then d = d'.
hypotheses: Squarefree is Mathlib's Squarefree on ℤ, so ±1 are squarefree and d may be negative.
The common value d c² is nonzero, so d, d' ≠ 0.
proofSteps: Signs: d c² and d' c'² have the signs of d and d', so d and d' have the same sign.

Valuations: for every prime p, v_p(d) + 2 v_p(c) = v_p(d') + 2 v_p(c') (padicValRat.mul, padicValRat.pow), and v_p(d), v_p(d') ∈ {0, 1} because d, d' are squarefree (Squarefree.natFactorization_le_one on |d|, |d'|); so v_p(d) = v_p(d').
Two nonzero integers with the same sign and the same valuation at every prime are equal (x = ±∏ p^{v_p(x)}).
acceptance: 2 · (3/2)² = 18 · (1/2)², but 18 is not squarefree; with squarefree data, 2 · c² = 2 · c'² forces c = ±c' and nothing else.
−3 · 2² = −12 = −3 · (−2)², while 3 · c² = −12 has no rational solution.

sources.match: The valuation on ℚ is additive and every nonzero rational is ±∏ p^{ν_p(x)}, which are the two facts the uniqueness compares.

nodes.title: The squarefree part is constant on square classes
nodes.statement: For nonzero rationals u and t, ratSquarefreePart(u t²) = ratSquarefreePart(u).
hypotheses: u, t ≠ 0; ratSquarefreePart is the parent's definition (the unique squarefree d with u = d c², c ≠ 0).
proofSteps: Write u = d c² with d = ratSquarefreePart u squarefree and c ≠ 0 (Rat.exists_squarefree_int_mul_sq and the parent's characterisation).
Then u t² = d (ct)² with ct ≠ 0, so by the signed uniqueness lemma ratSquarefreePart(u t²) = d.
acceptance: ratSquarefreePart(8/9) = ratSquarefreePart(2 · (2/3)²) = 2.
ratSquarefreePart(−12) = ratSquarefreePart(−3 · 2²) = −3.

sources.match: The valuation calculus behind the invariance under multiplication by squares.

nodes.title: A prime divides the squarefree part exactly when the valuation is odd
nodes.statement: For a nonzero rational u and a prime p, p divides ratSquarefreePart(u) if and only if padicValRat p u is odd.
hypotheses: u ≠ 0; p prime.
proofSteps: With u = d c², v_p(u) = v_p(d) + 2 v_p(c) (padicValRat.mul, padicValRat.pow), and v_p(d) ∈ {0, 1} because d is squarefree.
So v_p(u) is odd exactly when v_p(d) = 1, that is, when p divides d.
acceptance: For u = 8/9: v_2 = 3 is odd and 2 | 2; v_3 = −2 is even and 3 ∤ 2.
For u = −12: v_3 = 1 is odd and 3 | −3; v_2 = 2 is even and 2 ∤ −3.

sources.match: Additivity of ν_p on ℚ, from which the parity statement is read off.

nodes.title: The coordinate criterion for primary Eisenstein integers
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field with IsCyclotomicExtension {3} ℚ K and ω ∈ 𝓞_K a primitive cube root of unity. For a, b ∈ ℤ, a + bω is primary (≡ 2 mod 3𝓞_K) if and only if a ≡ 2 (mod 3) and b ≡ 0 (mod 3).
hypotheses: The coordinates are those of the ℤ-basis {1, ω} of 𝓞_K.
proofSteps: {1, ω} is a ℤ-basis of 𝓞_K (integralPowerBasisOfPrimePow for 3 = 3^1, whose generator is ω and whose dimension is φ(3) = 2).
Hence 3𝓞_K = 3ℤ ⊕ 3ℤω, and a + bω − 2 ∈ 3𝓞_K exactly when 3 | a − 2 and 3 | b.
acceptance: −1 − 3ω is primary; 2 + ω and 3 + ω are not.
−ω² = 1 + ω is not primary (a = 1).

sources.match: A prime a + bω is primary when a ≡ 2 and b ≡ 0 (mod 3), the coordinate form of π ≡ 2 (mod 3).
π primary means π ≡ 2 (mod 3), read in the coordinates a + bζ_3.

nodes.title: Every Eisenstein prime of norm different from 3 has exactly one primary associate
nodes.statement: Let K = ℚ(ζ_3) with 𝓞_K = ℤ[ω]. Every prime π of 𝓞_K with N(π) ≠ 3 has exactly one primary associate, among the six associates uπ, u ∈ {±1, ±ω, ±ω²}.
hypotheses: π prime with N(π) ≠ 3, so π is prime to 1 − ω and N(π) ≡ 1 (mod 3).
proofSteps: The units of 𝓞_K are ±1, ±ω, ±ω² (IsCyclotomicExtension.Rat.Three.Units.mem).

Existence: for π = a + bω, a² − ab + b² = N(π) ≡ 1 (mod 3); the six associates a + bω, −b + (a − b)ω, (b − a) − aω, −a − bω, b + (b − a)ω, (a − b) + aω cover the cases 3 ∤ a or 3 ∤ b, and the coordinate criterion selects one with first coordinate ≡ 2 and second ≡ 0 (mod 3).
Uniqueness: if π and uπ are both ≡ 2 (mod 3), then (u − 1)π ∈ 3𝓞_K; π is prime to 3, so 3 | u − 1, and among the six units only u = 1 satisfies this (u − 1 is 0, a unit, or of norm 3 or 4).
acceptance: The primary associate of 3 + ω (norm 7) is (a − b) + aω = 2 + 3ω, the complex conjugate of the primary prime −1 − 3ω.
2 is its own primary associate; 1 − ω (norm 3) has none.

sources.match: Lists the six associates of a + bζ_3 and proves existence and uniqueness of the primary one when N(π) = p ≡ 1 (mod 3).
States that every prime of norm different from 3 has exactly one primary associate.

nodes.title: The cubic Jacobi sum of a primary prime is primary
nodes.statement: Let π be a primary prime of ℤ[ω] of norm p ≡ 1 (mod 3) and χ = (·/π)_3. Then J(χ, χ) ≡ 2 (mod 3𝓞_K).
hypotheses: As in the parent's Jacobi sum lemma.
proofSteps: In the ring of integers R of ℚ(ω, ζ_p), g(χ)^3 = pJ(χ, χ) (the cubic Gauss sum identity).
Modulo 3R, cubing is additive: g(χ)^3 ≡ Σ_t χ(t)^3 ψ(t)^3 = Σ_{t ≠ 0} ψ(3t) = −1, since χ^3 = 1 on 𝔽_pˣ and 3 is invertible in 𝔽_p.
As p ≡ 1 (mod 3), J ≡ −1 ≡ 2 (mod 3R), and 3R ∩ 𝓞_K = 3𝓞_K (an element of K integral over ℤ lies in 𝓞_K).

sources.match: Shows J(χ_π, χ_π) ≡ −1 (mod 3) from g^3 = pJ and the congruence g^3 ≡ −1.
The same congruence as the first part of the proof that J = π.

nodes.title: The cube of the Gauss sum of a cubic character
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field with q elements, R an integral domain, χ : F → R a multiplicative character of order exactly 3 and ψ a primitive additive character of F with values in R. Then χ(−1) = 1 and g(χ, ψ)^3 = q · J(χ, χ).
hypotheses: orderOf χ = 3; ψ primitive; R a domain (χ(−1) is then a root of unity of order dividing 2 and 3).
proofSteps: gaussSum_pow_eq_prod_jacobiSum with orderOf χ = 3 gives g(χ)^3 = χ(−1) · q · ∏_{i ∈ Ico 1 2} J(χ, χ^i) = χ(−1) · q · J(χ, χ).
acceptance: For χ = (·/π)_3 with π = −1 − 3ω of norm 7: g^3 = 7 J(χ, χ) = 7π.
The identity fails for a quadratic character (order 2), where g² = χ(−1) q: the order hypothesis is used.

sources.match: g(χ_π)^3 = pJ(χ_π, χ_π) from the Gauss–Jacobi relation and χ_π(−1) = 1.
The general identity g(χ)^m = χ(−1) p J(χ, χ) ⋯ J(χ, χ^{m−2}) for a character of order m, specialised here to m = 3.

nodes.title: The cubic Jacobi sum has norm p and is divisible by π
nodes.statement: Let π be a primary prime of ℤ[ω] of norm p ≡ 1 (mod 3) and χ = (·/π)_3. Then J(χ, χ) times its complex conjugate is p, and π divides J(χ, χ) in 𝓞_K. Consequently J(χ, χ) = π.
hypotheses: As in the parent's Jacobi sum lemma; 𝓞_K = ℤ[ω] is a principal ideal domain.
proofSteps: J(χ, χ) J(χ⁻¹, χ⁻¹) = p (jacobiSum_mul_jacobiSum_inv; χ, χ and χ² are nontrivial), and J(χ⁻¹, χ⁻¹) = J(χ̄, χ̄) is the complex conjugate.
Modulo π, χ(t) ≡ t^{(p−1)/3}, so J ≡ Σ_t t^k(1 − t)^k with k = (p − 1)/3, a combination of power sums Σ_t t^j with 1 ≤ j ≤ 2k < p − 1, all zero (FiniteField.sum_pow_lt_card_sub_one); so π | J.
J has norm p and is divisible by π (norm p), so J is an associate of π (𝓞_K is a PID, three_pid); J is primary (previous lemma), and π has exactly one primary associate, so J = π.
acceptance: For π = −1 − 3ω: J(χ, χ) = −1 − 3ω, and its conjugate 2 + 3ω satisfies (−1 − 3ω)(2 + 3ω) = 7.
The non-primary associate −π gives the same character, so J = π, not −π.

sources.match: Shows J J̄ = p and J ≡ 0 (mod π) by the power-sum argument, and concludes J = π from primarity.
The same three steps: primary congruence, norm p, divisibility by π.

nodes.title: The cubic symbol of a rational integer at a rational prime is trivial
nodes.statement: Let q ≡ 2 (mod 3) be a rational prime (inert in ℤ[ω]) and n a rational integer prime to q. Then (n/q)_3 = 1. In particular cubic reciprocity holds trivially for two distinct rational primes q₁, q₂ ≡ 2 (mod 3).
hypotheses: q ≡ 2 (mod 3) prime, so q is a primary prime of ℤ[ω] of norm q²; n ∈ ℤ prime to q.
proofSteps: Complex conjugation fixes n and q, so by Galois equivariance conj((n/q)_3) = (n/q)_3.
For a cube root of unity ζ, conj(ζ) = ζ² ; so (n/q)_3 = (n/q)_3², and (n/q)_3 = 1.

sources.match: Proves χ_p(n) = 1 for rational n prime to p from χ_π(ᾱ) = χ̄_π(α) and the fact that a cube root of unity's conjugate is its square.

sources.locator: §3, proof of Theorem 3.1, first case, p. 64
sources.match: The case of two rational primes.

nodes.title: Cubic reciprocity between a rational prime and a complex primary prime
nodes.statement: Let q ≡ 2 (mod 3) be a rational prime and π a primary prime of ℤ[ω] of norm p ≡ 1 (mod 3). Then (q/π)_3 = (π/q)_3.
hypotheses: q ≠ p automatically (p ≡ 1, q ≡ 2 mod 3).
proofSteps: In R = 𝓞 of ℚ(ω, ζ_p): g(χ_π)^3 = pπ (the cubic Gauss sum lemma). Raise to (q² − 1)/3 and reduce modulo q: g^{q²−1} ≡ (pπ)^{(q²−1)/3} ≡ (pπ/q)_3 = (π/q)_3, since (p/q)_3 = 1 by the previous lemma.
Also g^{q²} ≡ Σ_t χ_π(t)^{q²} ψ(t)^{q²} = Σ_t χ_π(t) ψ(q²t) = χ_π(q⁻²) g = χ_π(q) g (mod q), by the Frobenius congruence (gaussSum_frob), q² ≡ 1 (mod 3) and the shift formula (gaussSum_mulShift_eq).
g is invertible modulo q (g ḡ = p), so (π/q)_3 ≡ χ_π(q) (mod q); two cube roots of unity congruent modulo q are equal.
acceptance: q = 2, π = −1 − 3ω: (2/π)_3 = ω² = (π/2)_3 (the parent's acceptance example).

sources.match: Compares g^{q²−1} computed from g³ = pπ with g^{q²} computed by the Frobenius congruence.

sources.locator: §3, proof of Theorem 3.1, second case, pp. 64–65
sources.match: The same comparison.

nodes.title: Cubic reciprocity between two complex primary primes
nodes.statement: Let π₁, π₂ be primary primes of ℤ[ω] of norms p₁ ≠ p₂, both ≡ 1 (mod 3). Then (π₂/π₁)_3 = (π₁/π₂)_3.
hypotheses: p₁ ≠ p₂, so π₁ and π₂ are coprime and neither divides the other's norm.
proofSteps: As in the previous lemma, in the ring of integers of ℚ(ω, ζ_{p₁}) and modulo a prime above π₂: g(χ_{π₁})^{p₂} ≡ χ_{π₁}(p₂)⁻¹ g(χ_{π₁}) = χ_{π₁}(p₂²) g(χ_{π₁}), while g(χ_{π₁})^{p₂−1} = (p₁π₁)^{(p₂−1)/3} ≡ χ_{π₂}(p₁π₁); so χ_{π₁}(p₂²) = χ_{π₂}(p₁π₁). Symmetrically χ_{π₂}(p₁²) = χ_{π₁}(p₂π₂).
Write x = χ_{π₁}(π₂), y = χ_{π₂}(π₁), u = χ_{π₁}(π̄₂), v = χ_{π₂}(π̄₁), using p₁ = π₁π̄₁ and p₂ = π₂π̄₂: the two relations read x²u² = y²v and y²v² = x²u.
Multiplying them gives uv = 1; substituting v = u⁻¹ in the first gives x² u³ = y², and u³ = 1, so x² = y²; squaring is a bijection of μ_3, so x = y.
acceptance: π₁ = −1 − 3ω (norm 7) and π₂ = −1 + 3ω (norm 13): modulo π₁, ω ≡ 2 and π₂ ≡ 5 with 5² ≡ 4 ≡ ω²; modulo π₂, ω ≡ 9 and π₁ ≡ 11 with 11⁴ ≡ 3 ≡ ω²; both symbols are ω².

sources.match: Derives the two congruences and combines them with χ_π(ᾱ) = conj(χ_π(α)).

sources.locator: §3, proof of Theorem 3.1, third case, pp. 65–66
sources.match: The same argument.

nodes.title: Cubic reciprocity between a primary prime and a rational integer
nodes.statement: Let π be a primary prime of ℤ[ω] with N(π) ≠ 3, and A a rational integer prime to 3 and to π. Then (A/π)_3 = (π/A)_3, the right side being the cubic symbol at the ideal A ℤ[ω].
hypotheses: A ∈ ℤ, 3 ∤ A, A prime to π; A may be negative or composite. (−1/·)_3 = 1 because −1 = (−1)³.
proofSteps: Both sides are unchanged by A ↦ −A, so take A > 0 and factor A into rational primes q ≡ 2 (mod 3), which are primary primes of ℤ[ω], and p ≡ 1 (mod 3) = ρρ̄ with ρ, ρ̄ primary primes of norm p (conjugation preserves π ≡ 2 mod 3).
(A/π) = ∏ (q/π) ∏ (ρ/π)(ρ̄/π) and (π/A) = ∏ (π/q) ∏ (π/ρ)(π/ρ̄) (multiplicativity in numerator and in the ideal).

Each factor pair agrees by cubic reciprocity: for a rational prime factor q (and π rational or complex) by the two previous lemmas; for ρ, ρ̄ by the two-complex-primes lemma, their norm p differing from N(π) because otherwise π would be associate to ρ or ρ̄ and divide A.

sources.locator: §3, Williams' proof of the supplement, pp. 66–67
sources.match: Applies cubic reciprocity with the composite primary rational denominators a and a + b; the node is that multiplicative extension, which the review asked to be stated separately.
Cubic reciprocity for primary primes of distinct norms, the input of the multiplicative extension.

nodes.title: The unique root of unity making a cyclotomic integer primary
nodes.statement: Let l be an odd prime, K = ℚ(ζ_l), ζ = ζ_l ∈ 𝓞_K and λ = 1 − ζ. Then λ𝓞_K is a prime of residue degree 1 with 𝓞_K/λ ≅ 𝔽_l; every α ∈ 𝓞_K satisfies α ≡ a + bλ (mod λ²) for some a, b ∈ ℤ, unique modulo l; ζ^c ≡ 1 − cλ (mod λ²) for c ∈ ℤ; and for α prime to l there is exactly one c ∈ ℤ/l such that ζ^c α is primary (congruent to a rational integer modulo λ²).
hypotheses: l odd prime; α prime to l means λ ∤ α.
proofSteps: λ is prime (IsPrimitiveRoot.zeta_sub_one_prime') of residue degree 1 (IsCyclotomicExtension.Rat.inertiaDeg_span_zeta_sub_one), so α ≡ a (mod λ) for some a ∈ ℤ, and (α − a)/λ ≡ b (mod λ) for some b ∈ ℤ: α ≡ a + bλ (mod λ²).
ζ^c = (1 − λ)^c ≡ 1 − cλ (mod λ²), so ζ^c α ≡ a + (b − ac)λ (mod λ²).

If λ ∤ α then l ∤ a, so there is exactly one c modulo l with ac ≡ b (mod l), i.e. with ζ^c α ≡ a (mod λ²); uniqueness uses that a + eλ with e ∈ ℤ is congruent to a rational integer modulo λ² exactly when l | e (λ² ∩ ℤ = lℤ for l odd).
acceptance: For α = ζ = 1 − λ: a = 1, b = −1, and the unique c is −1 (ζ^{−1}ζ = 1).
α = 2 is primary (c = 0); α = 1 − ζ is not prime to l.

sources.match: Proves α ≡ a + b(1 − ζ_l), ζ^d ≡ 1 − d(1 − ζ_l) modulo (1 − ζ_l)², and the existence and uniqueness of the normalising power.

restructure.detail: CA.1 now has 34 first-pass nodes and 41 continuation nodes, with ten candidate planets (six first-pass, four here) against the atlas limit of six per layer. Its material falls into three directions with few edges between them: elementary residues and quadratic characters; the local norm-residue symbol with the power reciprocity law; and the explicit higher laws (cubic, quartic, Eisenstein) proved by Gauss and Jacobi sums.

sourceIssues.printed: The coordinate criterion is printed as: a nonunit a + bi is primary if and only if either a ≡ 1 (mod 4) and b ≡ 0 (mod 4), or a ≡ 3 (mod 4), with no condition on b in the second case.
sourceIssues.correction: A nonunit a + bi is primary if and only if a ≡ 1, b ≡ 0 (mod 4) or a ≡ 3, b ≡ 2 (mod 4).
sourceIssues.reason: 3 = 3 + 0i has a ≡ 3 (mod 4) but is not ≡ 1 modulo (1 + i)^3: 3 − 1 = 2 has norm 4 < 8. Writing 1 + (2 + 2i)(x + yi) = (1 + 2x − 2y) + 2(x + y)i shows that b ≡ 2 (mod 4) is forced when a ≡ 3 (mod 4).

sourceIssues.printed: The prime factorisation of Gauss sums (Lemmas 2–3, Propositions 2–4) is proved for an odd prime p, but Proposition 5 (Stickelberger's theorem for an abelian field) applies Proposition 4 to every prime divisor of an ideal A prime to m, including the primes above 2 when m is odd.
sourceIssues.correction: The factorisation (g(χ)^m) = ℘^{Σ a σ_a⁻¹} also holds for p = 2: there ζ_2 = −1, ℚ(ζ_m, ζ_2) = ℚ(ζ_m) and the prime above ℘ is ℘ itself; lifting Tr(a) to {0, 1}, (−1)^{Tr(a)} = 1 − 2 Tr(a), so g(ω⁻¹) is 2 times an element ≡ q − 1 ≢ 0 modulo the prime, and s(1) = 1 because 2 is unramified in ℚ(ζ_{q−1}); Lemma 2 and Proposition 2 then hold with p − 1 = 1.
sourceIssues.reason: The proof of Lemma 3 expands ζ_p = 1 + π to first order in π with π of valuation 1 above p in a ramified extension; for p = 2 that extension is trivial and the expansion is exact, so the statement survives but the written proof does not cover the case.

sourceIssues.printed: The proof opens by deducing from Lemma 6.18 that (α)^γ ≡ ±1 (mod l).

sourceIssues.printed: The proof writes 1 − a as the product of the n factors 1 − ζ^i ⁿ√a and concludes that 1 − a is a norm from K(ⁿ√a).
sourceIssues.correction: When K(ⁿ√a) has degree d < n over K the product is not a single norm of 1 − ⁿ√a; grouping the n factors into n/d blocks of d conjugates shows 1 − a = ∏_{i < n/d} N_{K(ⁿ√a)/K}(1 − ζ_n^i ⁿ√a), still a norm.
sourceIssues.reason: The conjugates of ⁿ√a over K are its products with the d-th roots of unity only, so N_{K(ⁿ√a)/K}(1 − ⁿ√a) is the product of d of the n factors, not of all n; for 1 < d < n the conclusion needs the grouping into n/d norms (Fesenko–Vostokov IV.5.1, proof of (2)).
